transcript:
Header: 2026-12-28 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Priya (Zenith CTO), Mark (Lead ML Eng), Olga (Infra), Evan (SRE)

Summary: quick recap at the end with next steps and deliverables. Shared artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/zenith-latency), security doc pointer, KV warmup script.

[00:00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining; quick intro, i'm Samira from Redwood, with Luis our systems SE. we got your note about p99 spikes — want to walk through what we saw and then dig into your traces. priya, do you want to kick off with your current symptoms?

[00:00:25] Priya: yeah thanks, um, hi. so we're seeing occasional p99s up to ~1.8s on short-chat prompts that usually land at ~120ms p95. it's pretty visible on peak traffic windows. would like to get that down to sub-500ms p99 for the assistant product.

[00:00:48] Luis: ok got it. when you say short-chat prompts, what's the token count distribution? are these single-turn, short responses?

[00:01:05] Mark: mostly 8-30 tokens generated, with user messages 5-20 tokens. traffic is bursty — events, sudden concurrent sessions. our setup is in a VPC in us-west-2, we hit your dedicated endpoint via PrivateLink, tls terminated at the redwood edge, then into a private subnet.

[00:01:28] Olga: and we do some internal rate-limiting at the api gateway. also FYI we tried reducing concurrency per-conn but didn't help much.

[00:01:40] Luis: cool, that helps. two high-level sources for tail: 1) serving runtime contention (hot shards, batching artifacts), 2) network hops / cold KV cache, and 3) model kernel path due to quantization fallbacks or cross-architecture kernel selection.

[00:02:10] Samira: or as we often say, p95 is often the happy path, p99 is where you see the cold-starts and the weird network jitter. we'll go through traces and some mitigations — batching settings, KV cache prewarm, and reducing hops.

[00:02:36] Priya: the traces we uploaded show a repeated pattern: an extra ~400ms between our VPC egress and the first server recv time, and sometimes a 250ms gap mid-request. looks like a TLS handshake occasionally, or maybe a misrouted request?

[00:02:58] Luis: couple quick clarifications — PrivateLink typically avoids cross-az egress, but if your endpoint's DNS resolves to multiple IPs we can, in rare cases, land on different infra causing extra hops. also TLS renegotiation can happen if connections are short-lived; do you reuse keep-alives?

[00:03:18] Mark: we set keep-alive to 30s, but client side is a lambda with ephemeral containers, so connections die. we do see a lot of new tcp handshakes in the p99 traces.

[00:03:34] Luis: that's a big one — new TCP/TLS handshake adds ~80-150ms typically, but in some congested paths it can exceed that. for short responses (10-20ms server time) the handshake dominates. streaming can help here because you can start a chunk earlier, but streaming also needs more frequent flushes which can interact with batching.

[00:04:05] Samira: ok let's separate streaming vs non-streaming impacts: streaming improves perceived latency to the first token — you see answer sooner — but it changes how we batch inside the runtime. continuous-batching means the runtime waits for a small window to group requests; with streaming, we can flush tokens earlier which reduces perceived latency but sometimes increases p99 if flush timers or scheduling conflicts cause extra waits.

[00:04:36] Priya: interesting — so streaming could help user perceived latency but might not fix the p99 if the network handshake is the issue.

[00:04:45] Luis: exactly. if your dominant tail cause is network cold-connections, first fix is connection reuse or fronting with a warm proxy. second is co-locating a small pool of requesters (or using a long-lived sidecar) to keep TLS alive. third, we can look at edge placement.

[00:05:10] Olga: what about KV cache? we heard that Redwood has prefix cache and KV cache — how does that affect tails?

[00:05:23] Luis: the KV cache (our term for key-value attention cache) is critical for chat; a cold KV cache causes full context recompute which explodes latency. warm KV caches keep the model's KV shard in GPU memory and avoid disk or re-sync. typical cold miss penalty is 200-800ms depending on model and sequence length. in your traces i see some misses aligned with new session ids.

[00:05:55] Mark: yes a pattern of session churn — our upstream creates new session ids per user open. any recommendations?

[00:06:04] Luis: two paths: 1) session affinity / sticky routing so same user lands on same serving shard, or 2) KV-cache warmup on session creation. we have a warmup script that issues a small prefix request to populate the cache. also we can do prefix-preservation — keep short common prompts cached across sessions.

[00:06:28] Samira: we'll share the KV warmup script — luis will upload to the shared drive. for a pilot we recommend pinning a small dedicated pool and enabling sticky routing for sample users to see p99 improvements quickly.

[00:06:42] Priya: what about batching settings — we currently use dynamic batching with max-batch 64, max-wait 12ms. we thought increasing wait might help throughput but worried about latency.

[00:06:58] Luis: dynamic batching tradeoff: higher max-wait increases throughput and reduces avg cost but widens p95/p99. continuous batching (also called continuous aggregation) is another mode where the runtime does per-model micro-batches and can do early flush for small tokens. for real-time short responses, we usually recommend lower max-wait (6-10ms) and rely on dedicated pool to absorb throughput. if you need to save cost, increase batch size but accept p99 impact.

[00:07:31] Mark: are there kernel-level things? like sometimes i see a fallback kernel path that runs slower, maybe float fallback for int8.

[00:07:41] Luis: yes — quantization profile and kernel selection matter. int8/int4 quantized paths give big speedups but occasionally certain ops have no optimized kernel on some GPUs/RT kernels, which triggers a slower path (float fallback) and causes tail spikes. in our onboarding we run a kernel coverage test; if we see fallback frequency >2% on your prompt set we advise either switching to a different quant profile or using a different GPU type or a mixed strategy (hot-models int8, fallbacks served by a float replica).

[00:08:13] Priya: ok. so for our pilot should we use int8 or float32?

[00:08:18] Samira: typical recommendation: start with int8 if quality is acceptable on your eval set to lower token cost and improve throughput, but for stringent p99 SLOs we sometimes run a small float replica in the dedicated pool to handle the paths that quantization can't accelerate. we'll include quant recommendations in the docs.

[00:08:36] Olga: network-wise, you mentioned PrivateLink vs VPC peering — any measurable differences?

[00:08:44] Luis: PrivateLink usually reduces blast radius and avoids exposing public IPs, but it adds an extra network hop through the regional endpoint infrastructure — that can add ~5-20ms median but sometimes more under load. VPC peering is lower hop count but needs cross-account routes and is less flexible. The real issue for p99 is cross-AZ traffic and sudden route changes. we saw in your trace a cross-az handoff that aligns with spikes.

[00:09:15] Mark: can we force AZ affinity?

[00:09:20] Luis: yes, with subnet-level endpoint selection and client-side affinity you can bias traffic to a single AZ. coupled with connection reuse, that reduces inter-AZ jitter.

[00:09:30] Samira: also consider using our edge keepwarm — an optional long-lived TLS proxy colocated in your VPC that keeps connections hot to Redwood and amortizes handshake cost. it adds a managed sidecar but usually improves p99 for lambda-like clients.

[00:09:48] Priya: what's the expected improvement numbers? rough ballpark if we enable sticky routing + dedicated pool + KV warmup?

[00:09:56] Luis: ballpark: you could see p99 drop from ~1.8s to 400-600ms for those short prompts if the network handshake is the main cause. if cold KV misses dominate, the warmup and affinity can get you to ~300-500ms. exact depends on prompt shapes and concurrency.

[00:10:20] Evan: quick question — streaming vs non-streaming, when you recommend streaming and when not to?

[00:10:27] Luis: streaming is great for perceived latency (time to first token). for multi-utterance assistants it's good. but if you have strict p99 for end-to-end response we need to tune flush windows and batching; sometimes non-streaming with aggressive batching and lower max-wait yields lower p99 for final token. it really depends on UX.

[00:10:47] Mark: do you have instrumentation hooks so we can see per-component latency (network, edge, runtime, kv-cache)?

[00:10:55] Samira: yeah the Redwood Console trace includes token-level breakdown: ingress, TLS handshake, scheduling, kernel exec, and kv-cache hit/miss. we'll grant you a view and attach sample dashboards to the pilot.

[00:11:10] Priya: we saw a recurring 200-300ms 'scheduling' step in some traces — is that the batching window?

[00:11:17] Luis: scheduling can be batching wait, or queueing because a particular GPU shard is hot. if you have hot keys (same user with large context), it can cause head-of-line blocking for other small requests. we have strategies: shard balancing, per-route capacity, and small fast-path replicas for short sequences.

[00:11:42] Samira: for the pilot we'll propose a small two-tier cluster: a few fast small-context replicas and the larger general-purpose pool. that reduces interference.

[00:11:55] Mark: what's the effort to set up sticky routing? do we change our client or is it on your side?

[00:12:02] Luis: we support both: client-side affinity via a session cookie or a header, or we can do routing in the control plane if you share your session mapping. it's pretty light on infra changes.

[00:12:13] Priya: show of hands — is there anything else in the traces that looks weird?

[00:12:18] Luis: one more thing — we saw occasional CPU-side spikes at the edge service doing JSON parsing/acl checks — that's a 30-80ms hit when payloads are large. trimming headers and using smaller auth tokens or signing can mitigate.

[00:12:35] Olga: noted. we'll check payload sizes.

[00:12:40] Samira: ok let's go through a quick prioritized mitigations list: 1) reduce TLS cold handshakes (connection reuse, edge keepwarm), 2) KV-cache warmup & sticky routing, 3) dedicated pool with two tiers, 4) tweak batching (lower max-wait for short responses), 5) quantization + optional float replica for fallback paths, 6) AZ affinity and endpoint tuning.

[00:13:14] Priya: sounds good. how will we measure pilot success? our internal SLO is p99 < 500ms for 90% of endpoints for these short prompts.

[00:13:26] Samira: we'll propose pilot SLOs and measurement windows. recommended: run a 2-week A/B where 10% of production traffic is pinned to the dedicated pool with warmups, measure p95/p99 and cost delta. if we meet p99 targets we can expand.

[00:13:44] Mark: do you have any scripts to generate realistic bursty traffic? our data's funky to reproduce.

[00:13:51] Luis: yes — benchmark spreadsheet contains a burst generator and traffic envelope for lambda-like clients. i'll add a sample terraform to spin a warm proxy as well. link will be in the shared drive.

[00:14:10] Priya: any security or compliance blockers for PrivateLink and edge keepwarm?

[00:14:16] Samira: PrivateLink is fine for most compliance; edge keepwarm runs in your VPC as a managed container so keys don't leave your network. we'll include SOC2/ISO artifacts in the security packet.

[00:14:30] Olga: good. one last thing — quantization regression monitoring. we want to avoid quality regressions if switching to int8.

[00:14:38] Luis: we recommend a small eval harness tied to prompt sets and diff-based quality alerts. Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and send regression alerts if a change crosses thresholds. we'll include setup steps.

[00:14:55] Samira: great — quick recap and owners: samira pricing and contract, luis benchmarks + scripts, mark to send prompts and histograms. any other blockers?

[00:15:05] Priya: no blockers. timeline — we want pilot in january.

[00:15:10] Samira: ok we'll target a pilot kickoff week of 2027-01-11. we'll send the runbook beforehand.

[00:15:18] Luis: i'll upload the KV warmup and the benchmark scripts; also will include notes on how to configure the dedicated pool and the two-tier replica strategy.

[00:15:26] Mark: appreciate it.

[00:15:30] Samira: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a summary email and the shared links.

[00:15:35] (call continues with a short Q&A about pricing tiers and contract terms; lower-priority discussion omitted)

[00:40:00] Samira: closing notes — prices for dedicated small pilot and estimated cost delta for two-tier setup will be in the proposal.

[00:57:30] Samira: final wrap, thanks all.
